IMPLEMENTATION REVIEW

9 Oct 2026 · 10 current branch snapshots

How the scores work

These are editorial judgments about the implementations at the linked commits, including later fixes. They are not measurements of model capability or ratings of the original one-shot commits.

Each category is scored from 0 to 10. Overall is their arithmetic mean, rounded to one decimal. Cards sort by that displayed overall score, then prompt completeness, then game design. Scores around 9 indicate strong implementation with minor gaps; 7–8 indicates a solid result with material weaknesses; 4–6 indicates a partial game; 0–3 indicates fundamental blockers or unfinished systems.

Game design
Playability, fairness, feedback, pacing, visual readability, and how the mall and store mechanics work together.
Code architecture
Separation of rules and presentation, state ownership, determinism, module boundaries, and integration between systems.
Code design
Algorithms, data models, APIs, collision and input handling, correctness, and how easily the implementation can be extended.
Code cleanliness
Readability, naming, formatting, duplication, useful comments, type discipline, and removal of unfinished or disconnected code.
Prompt completeness
Working coverage of the original prompt: traversal, packages, stores, enemies, extras, power-ups, screens, audio, art, input, and technical constraints.

Review scope

The review compared source, assets, tests, build configuration, and gameplay rules with the original prompt. Every implementation's test suite and production build was run. Haiku 4.5 also received a separate TypeScript check because its build does not typecheck.

Browser checks sampled launch, title, arrival, and mall presentation. Stronger implementations also received store-entry checks using prepared player positions; Fable, GPT-6.1 and Haiku 5.5 received package-search checks, and Haiku 5.5 was also played in real time through elevator boarding, the map and pause, then stepped through an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. Targeted probes reproduced the Haiku 4.5 timing blocker, the Gemini store-exit blocker, and the Haiku 5.5 map-in-store, floor-blind wet-floor, power-up timer and Game Over shutter defects. GPT-6 Sol's dead-spy and Black Friday defects were reproduced in Node.

This was not an uninterrupted six-package walkthrough of all ten games. Unverified full-route completion is not claimed. Test counts are reported as context; they do not determine scores. Other findings come from source inspection and are described as inferences where relevant. Scores describe these source snapshots; published Play builds may change independently. The "written" date on each card is the day the model produced the implementation, taken from the branch README's benchmark notes or, where a README has none, from the branch's first commit.

Written 29 Sept 2026 · snapshot c15cebfb129a · branch sonnet-5-5

Game design
Detailed storefronts, lively characters, themed rooms, and clear search feedback make the caper feel coherent. Entry protection and guard delays improve fairness. Busy patterns and a dense HUD sometimes compete with the action.
Code architecture
A frame-driven Session owns the game flow; seeded rules and typed events are separated from browser, audio, and drawing. The boundaries are consistently exercised in Node. Some presentation state lives in the overlay rather than the simulation.
Code design
Input preserves printed-letter layouts and repeated taps; store movement, collision, searching, and guard behavior share explicit models. The roughly 1,200-line store module concentrates too many responsibilities despite otherwise focused modules.
Code cleanliness
Strict TypeScript, clear contracts, useful comments, and descriptive behavior tests make the implementation easy to follow. A few large modules and dense rendering code reduce local readability.
Prompt completeness
Very broad coverage of traversal, store extras, power-ups, generated art and music, and session screens. Its 477 tests include long seeded simulation runs. Sampled title, arrival, and store entry worked; this review did not establish a complete uninterrupted playthrough.

Verification

  • 477 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass; strict typecheck included.
  • Runtime: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed.

Source evidence: Session and state ownership · Store rules and collisions

Written 8 Oct 2026 · snapshot 1ec98345999f · branch haiku-5-5

Game design
The whole loop plays: zip-line arrival, elevators and escalators, timed searches with a progress bar, banners and popups, first-visit lines, level clear and harder loops, with telegraphed shots, store grace and respawn invulnerability for fairness. Opening the map inside a store leaves the room frozen on screen while the mall rules keep moving the agent, the wet-floor slide applies on every floor and can block the getaway wagon, timed power-ups never run out, and the Game Over screen ends fully covered by its shutters. Dark backdrops, abstract window displays and overflowing two-line signs make the mall less readable than the strongest entries.
Code architecture
Pure, seeded rules in core, mall and store modules emit typed events that a state-reading renderer and an audio layer consume; the input mapper and the splash are standalone and the browser shell is thin. The roughly 1,450-line mall module concentrates most behaviour, the game never ticks the power-up timers it owns, the map screen ignores which screen opened it, and banners persist across scene changes. Debug mode pauses real time, so the hooks cannot observe live play.
Code design
The elevator state machine, printed-letter input with exact key release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, and once-per-volley dodge rolls are well modelled. The wet-floor check ignores floors, closing the map inside a store returns to the mall with the room still attached, timed power-ups last until death, the shutter animation covers the Game Over text, and the room system is fixed at 16 by 11 tiles without a camera.
Code cleanliness
Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, short focused modules outside the mall world, readable names, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. Copy is duplicated inside rule modules despite the stated single-source rule, several sound effects, the shake output and some copy constants are defined but never used, and the README contradicts itself about the browser playtest.
Prompt completeness
Nearly every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, with 115 tests across the listed rule areas; the strict build and the published sub-path deployment work, and browser checks logged no console errors. Real-time play covered splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles; stepped checks covered store entry, a package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. The unticked power-up timers, the map inside stores, the floor-blind wet patch and the hidden Game Over text are working-coverage gaps; the room camera, photo strip and automatic-car ride are simplified.

Verification

  • 115 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass; strict typecheck included.
  • Runtime: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, map, pause and toggles passed; prepared store entry, package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over stepped; map-in-store, wet-floor and shutter defects reproduced.

Source evidence: Map screen returns to the mall · Wet-floor check without a floor · Power-up tick never called · Game Over shutters

Game design
The title, mall, and basic package loop are recognizable. Static sprites, simple rooms, and weak enemy behavior reduce the sense of a finished arcade game. Searching freezes store hazards, which distorts the intended risk and pacing.
Code architecture
Browser I/O, rendering, and seeded rules are separated, and updates clone state. Nearly all session, mall, and store rules are packed into one compressed module, with few explicit subsystem contracts.
Code design
A reproduced rule defect lets dead spies become active after their death timer expires. Black Friday shop generation leaves empty fixtures, guard movement ignores fixture collision, and the listening-booth geometry appears to prevent its activation. Cloning all state each tick adds unnecessary work.
Code cleanliness
Very long, densely compressed lines, single-letter locals, and combined responsibilities make inspection and safe changes difficult. The input module is more considered, but the overall source reads like a compressed prototype.
Prompt completeness
The basic screens and many named mechanics exist; all 25 tests and the build passed. Only six static gameplay sprites are defined, the CRT lacks real curvature, and several traversal, store, and power-up rules are partial or incorrect. The tests miss important gameplay defects.

Verification

  • 25 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass.
  • Runtime: Title, arrival and mall sampled; dead-spy and Black Friday defects reproduced in Node.

Game design
The mall renders and movement can be sampled, but essential progression is blocked. Store exits are unreachable, elevator movement does not carry the player, and minimal room art offers little feedback or atmosphere.
Code architecture
Logic, renderer, input, and synthesis are in separate modules. The boundary is weakened by non-seeded floating-text IDs, inconsistent private fixture data versus drawing, and incomplete integration of combat and traversal.
Code design
Store movement clamps the player's y position to 144 while exit requires more than 154; a browser probe reproduced the trap. Enemy bullets are created without a complete movement/collision path, and searches and fixtures lack the required collision and cancellation behavior.
Code cleanliness
Conventional formatting and recognizable module names make the scaffolding readable. Loose contracts, hardcoded room drawing, and unused or disconnected behavior obscure what actually works.
Prompt completeness
All 14 tests and the typechecked build passed, but essential traversal and combat, guards, many NPCs/extras, and distinct store experiences are missing or partial. The unreachable store exit prevents completing the requested package loop.

Verification

Written 29 Sept 2026 · snapshot d2b8c71ca66f · branch haiku-4-5

Game design
Normal launch stays on the first splash frame, including after Enter, so there is no usable player experience. Direct rule calls expose basic movement, but the store and traversal systems do not support the intended loop.
Code architecture
Modules suggest useful separation, but rules directly invoke audio, use unseeded randomness, and attach ad hoc store state. Elevator and power-up modules are not reliably integrated, and duplicate state fields disagree.
Code design
The main loop resets its timestamp whenever frame is zero, producing zero elapsed time forever. Elevator updates are not called by mall rules, store movement advances a tile per frame, and searches reveal contents immediately instead of running the specified timed interaction.
Code cleanliness
Formatting and straightforward names are readable. Placeholder comments, disconnected code, casts to any, and extensive TypeScript errors show that the pieces were not brought to a consistent finished state.
Prompt completeness
The 13 unit tests and Vite build passed, but a separate TypeScript check failed. The browser is stuck at frame zero; guards, collision, progression, and multiple extras are absent or incomplete. The existing tests exercise isolated rules and miss the broken entry point.

Verification

  • 13 tests passed.
  • Build: Vite build passes; separate TypeScript check fails.
  • Runtime: Splash remained at frame zero before and after Enter.

Source evidence: Broken browser timing loop · Rule integration · Store interactions
